rationale: Clinical AD patients are usually older than the non-AD comparison groups across these cohorts, and age is a strong prior for AD that the L2 protein model barely uses. This change keeps the protein logistic regression as it is. It then learns, on the training fold only, how to combine that model's score with age. To do that it gets out-of-fold protein scores from a 5-fold CV that keeps each subject's samples together (`GroupKFold` on `ctx["groups_train"]`), and fits a small 2-feature logistic regression on those scores plus standardized age.

With n≈137, the full ~1,500-protein L2 model is noisy. The published CSF proteomics AD signal is concentrated in a small set of proteins: the glycolysis enzymes PKM/ALDOA/GAPDH/ENO1/LDHB/MDH1, the 14-3-3 proteins YWHAG/YWHAZ, SMOC1, SPP1, the chitinases, and synaptic/neuronal markers. So I keep the current full model and average its probability with a strongly regularized logistic model on that prior biomarker panel. The panel model should have lower variance and add the biological prior.

CSF from four cohorts (Berlin, Sweden, Magdeburg, Kiel) carries strong per-site pre-analytical and batch shifts, and right now those shifts reach both logistic models untouched. On each training fold I fit a per-protein linear model of protein level on site plus diagnosis, then subtract only the estimated site offsets from train and test. This removes the cohort effect while keeping the disease signal, even when the AD fraction differs between sites.

rationale: This reruns the round-3 site-correction idea with the crash fixed; the score from the earlier attempt is unknown because it never ran. The crash came from 2-D indexing on a pandas Arrow string array. Site labels are now converted to a plain numpy string array first. On each training fold, a per-protein least-squares model of protein level on one-hot site plus diagnosis estimates site offsets. Those offsets are centred and subtracted from the training and test data before both logistic models. This removes cohort shifts but keeps the disease signal, even when the AD fraction differs between sites. Sites not seen in training get no shift, and the code falls back to no correction if site metadata is missing.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of whatever proteins it happened to detect. Detection is abundance-dependent, so samples with fewer quantified low-abundance proteins get a biased median, and that bias leaks into every protein value. This change centres each sample on the median of a fixed core set of proteins quantified in nearly all samples (≥95%, chosen without labels). It is a more stable estimate of how much total CSF protein was loaded into each run.

Published AD CSF proteomics signal comes as tightly co-regulated modules: glycolysis enzymes and 14-3-3 proteins go up, glial and inflammation markers go up, and synaptic/neurosecretory proteins such as NPTX2 and VGF go down. I add a third ensemble member: a lightly regularized logistic model on about 7 module scores. Each score is the mean of a module's standardized, site-adjusted proteins. With n≈137 this averages away per-protein measurement noise and is lower-variance than per-protein weights.

CSF samples carry different amounts of blood contamination from the lumbar puncture. Red-cell proteins such as haemoglobins, CA1 and PRDX2 then leak in and add a technical, sample-specific shift to many proteins, which Bader et al. flagged as a major confounder. This change builds a label-free contamination score for each sample and, on each training fold only, removes its per-protein effect in the same regression that removes site, keeping the diagnosis term in the model so disease signal is not removed.

Many CSF proteins change with normal ageing (for example through blood–CSF barrier permeability and glial activation), and some differ by sex. Neither effect is AD-specific, and both add per-sample variance. On each training fold, I now add standardized age and sex as nuisance covariates to the regression that already removes site offsets and blood contamination. Diagnosis stays in that regression as a term, so only the age/sex effect that is separate from diagnosis gets removed and the disease signal stays.

Missing values in this data depend on abundance, so for low-abundance proteins (e.g. neuronal/synaptic proteins) whether a protein was detected at all can carry disease information. Right now the full model throws away every protein quantified in fewer than 70% of training samples. This change adds a detected/not-detected indicator for each protein quantified in 20–70% of the training fold. The indicators go into the full L2 model and get the same per-fold site and blood-contamination adjustment as the protein levels, with diagnosis kept in that regression so its signal is not removed.

Many prior-panel proteins are low-abundance neuronal or glial markers, such as NEFL, NPTX2, VGF, NRGN, SNAP25, CHIT1 and TREM2. They are often only partly quantified, so the panel model either drops them (coverage below 50%) or fills in a half-minimum guess (50–70%). Round 9 showed that whether a protein was detected carries AD signal. So the panel model now also gets a detected/not-detected indicator for each panel protein quantified in 20–70% of the training fold. These indicators get the same per-fold site and blood-contamination adjustment as the protein levels.

I'm adding one change: after standardizing on the training fold, every feature is clipped to ±3 SD before both L2 logistic models. With n≈110 per fold, a few extreme values can dominate the fitted weights. Typical sources are half-minimum-imputed gaps in mostly quantified proteins (often 4–5 SD below the mean) and one-off pre-analytical artefacts. Clipping should make the linear AD signal more stable under small n.

In CSF, most plasma-derived proteins (albumin, immunoglobulins, fibrinogen, apolipoproteins, haptoglobin) get there by leaking through the blood–CSF barrier. How leaky that barrier is varies a lot between people, mainly with age and with other neurological conditions, and the effect is technical rather than AD-specific. Round 7 gained from removing blood contamination in the same way. This change adds a label-free barrier-leakage score and removes its per-protein effect inside the same per-fold regression as site and blood contamination. Diagnosis stays in that regression, so the disease signal is not removed.

The four cohorts were run as separate acquisition batches, so besides differing in mean level (already removed) they probably also differ in dynamic range and noise per protein. That is the "scale" part of a ComBat-style batch effect. This change adds a scale correction inside the per-fold regression. For each site and protein it estimates the residual spread with diagnosis, site and nuisance terms removed, shrinks that estimate toward the pooled spread to stabilise it at small n, and rescales protein levels within each site around the site's mean. This puts samples from different cohorts on comparable scales, and the disease effect is never used to estimate the scaling.

The full model spreads L2 weight over about 1,500 features, so with n≈110 per fold any strong AD proteins outside the prior panel get diluted by noise. I add a third ensemble member: an L2 logistic model on the 40 features with the strongest correlation to diagnosis. These come from the same site- and nuisance-adjusted protein levels plus detection indicators, and the selection is redone inside each training fold. This lets data-driven markers such as unlisted neuronal or glial proteins carry concentrated weight, and the full and panel models stay unchanged. I have not run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Platelet carry-over during lumbar puncture is a separate pre-analytical contamination axis from red-cell lysis and barrier leakage. It is one of the plasma/CSF sample-quality panels described by Geyer et al. and Bader et al. Following the two kept nuisance corrections (rounds 7 and 12), this change adds a label-free platelet-contamination score, built from platelet-specific proteins such as PF4, PPBP, ITGA2B/ITGB3, GP1BA and TUBB1. Its per-protein effect is removed in the same per-fold regression, with diagnosis kept as a term so the disease signal stays. I have not run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

The two regularization strengths are still hand-picked (C=0.05 for about 1,700 features, C=0.1 for about 50 panel proteins). With n≈110 per fold, how strong the penalty should be depends on how spread out the clinical-AD signal is, which we don't know. This change picks C for both the full model and the panel model with an inner StratifiedGroupKFold on each training fold, grouped by `ctx["groups_train"]`. Imputation, filtering, detection indicators and the site/nuisance adjustment are all rebuilt inside each inner split so nothing leaks. To cut selection noise, the choice uses pooled out-of-fold AUROC, smoothed across neighbouring C values. I have not run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

The ensemble currently averages the two members' probabilities. The full model (about 1,700 features, small C) and the panel model (about 50 features, larger C) have very different logit spreads, so whichever is more spread out silently dominates the ranking. Each member's logit is now standardised by the mean and SD of its inner-CV out-of-fold logits at the chosen C, and those standardised logits are averaged. This gives both members equal weight on their out-of-sample scale and keeps scores comparable across outer folds. I have not run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Removing known technical axes helped twice: blood contamination in round 7 and blood–CSF barrier leakage in round 12. That suggests other unmodelled sources of unwanted variation remain. This change estimates K=2 hidden factors with an SVA/RUV-style step, using the top principal components of the training-fold protein residuals after site, diagnosis and the two nuisance scores are regressed out, so the factors carry no diagnosis signal. It then removes those factors' per-protein effects in the same regression that handles site and nuisance. For test samples, the factor scores are estimated jointly with a free disease term, so test-time disease signal is not absorbed into the factors.

The full ridge model shrinks all ~1,700 features equally, so the ~50 prior AD biomarker proteins (glycolysis, 14-3-3, SMOC1, SPP1, chitinases, synaptic) are diluted by the noise features. This change multiplies the standardized panel features in the full model by a factor a ∈ {1, 2, 3}. That is the same as giving them a looser prior (penalty / a²), a Bayesian prior-informed ridge. Nested grouped inner CV picks the factor jointly with C. The panel member and everything else stay the same.

The full model scales every feature to unit variance, which inflates proteins near the noise floor that barely vary across samples. Pareto scaling (centre, then divide by √SD) is the usual proteomics/metabolomics middle ground: features that vary a lot between people, such as inflammatory and glial markers, keep more weight than measurement noise. Nested grouped inner CV now picks unit-variance or Pareto scaling together with C for the full model. Unit-variance scaling (the current setup) wins ties.
